note: An MIT-professor pass: every line teaches the mechanism, never reads the on-screen caption. No digits, symbols or code names; every number is spoken in words.

lines: Picture a small cache, every slot already holding something.
A fresh request arrives for something not yet inside, and the cache has to let one entry go before it can take the new one.
Stamp every entry with the moment it was last touched and finding the stalest one means checking every stamp — exactly the work a cache exists to avoid.
Split the job in two. One structure answers where is this, instantly; the other answers which one is oldest, instantly.
Neither does the other's job well on its own — a lookup table has no sense of order, and an ordered chain can't be searched quickly by key.
Put them together and a single lookup hands back not just a value, but a direct handle into the ordered chain, ready to move without searching for it.
Here's the trap. Reading a value out of the cache feels like it should leave everything else untouched.
But if the cache only remembers order from writes, a value that gets read constantly and never rewritten would look exactly as old as one nobody has touched in ages.
answer: It has to move — a plain lookup quietly becomes an update to the ordering structure.
That is the uncomfortable part: the busiest operation in the whole system is also the one doing bookkeeping work on every single call.

lines: Run that bookkeeping on a cache with a hundred slots, then again on one with tens of thousands, and count exactly how many internal links get rewritten each time.
The count doesn't move. Whatever the cache's size, touching one entry only ever touches its two immediate neighbours.
That's the entire payoff of pairing the two structures: a handle straight to the right spot means nothing downstream of it has to shift.
Now watch a short sequence of requests land on a cache that can only hold a few things at once.
Some keys repeat. Follow one of them closely: does it survive long enough to still be sitting there the second time it's asked for, or has something already pushed it out?
Suppose every thread touching this cache has to grab the same lock just to slide one entry to the front.
At that point the ordering structure, not the actual lookup, becomes the bottleneck.
What if the cache gave up remembering the exact order altogether, and settled for something rougher but far cheaper to update?
answer: Approximate the order instead of keeping it exact.
Give up knowing precisely which of several recently touched entries came last, and in exchange make the per-touch cost almost disappear.

lines: Here's the rougher version: one flag per entry, flipped on whenever it's touched, and a single pointer that sweeps around all the entries in a fixed circle.
A touch costs nothing more than flipping that one flag. Choosing a victim means the sweeping pointer walking forward, turning off any flag it finds lit, until it lands on one already dark.
Run it on the very same request sequence as the exact version, and the two throw out almost the same entries — the rough version loses almost nothing here, for a touch that costs far less.
Now imagine something unusual passes through: a one-time job that reads a huge run of entries, each exactly once, far more than the cache could ever hold.
From the cache's point of view, every one of those reads looks identical to a normal, meaningful touch.
So does the stuff that was genuinely popular before that job started survive it, or does the job itself count as the most recent activity everywhere?
answer: It gets pushed out — a rule built only on recency has no way to tell 'used once by something huge' apart from 'used constantly.'
Both look like the newest touch at the moment they happen, and that's all a purely recency-based rule can see.

lines: Measure the hit rate right after that huge one-time job finishes, and compare it to the same short window with no such job beforehand.
Under the exact ordering version and under the rough, flag-based version alike, that rate drops hard, right after the intrusion — the popular stuff really is gone.

A third approach gives up tracking order at all, just a timestamp and a few random guesses at eviction time, and it does a little worse still on ordinary traffic — the price of carrying almost no structure whatsoever.
Pulling the three apart: pairing a lookup table with an ordered chain gives an exact answer, at the cost of touching that chain on every single read.
Swapping in a flag and a sweeping pointer keeps nearly the same accuracy while making that per-read cost almost disappear.
But notice what none of them solved: a single oversized, one-time pass still wrecks either approach, because both are built entirely out of recency and nothing else.
